q: Let $f:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$ satisfy $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all rational $x,y$. (i) Show that $f(0)=0$ and $f(-x)=-f(x)$. (ii) Show that $f(nx)=nf(x)$ for every integer $n$. (iii) Deduce that $f(x)=cx$ for all rational $x$, where $c=f(1)$. (iv) Now let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y)$ for all real $x,y$, and suppose also that $g$ is increasing. Show that $g(x)=cx$ for all real $x$.

(i) Show that $\ln x\le x-1$ for all $x>0$, with equality only at $x=1$. (ii) Let $a_1,\dots,a_n>0$ have arithmetic mean $A$. By applying (i) to each $a_i/A$, prove the AM-GM inequality $A\ge\sqrt[n]{a_1a_2\cdots a_n}$. (iii) Show that $\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n<e$ for every positive integer $n$. (iv) By applying (i) to $1/x$, show that $\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n+1}>e$. Deduce that $\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n\to e$.

Consider the equation $x^2-kx+k+3=0$, where $k$ is real. (i) For which $k$ does the equation have real roots? (ii) For which $k$ are both roots real and positive? (iii) For which $k$ do the roots differ by exactly 1? (iv) Find all $k$ for which both roots are integers.
Prove that for every positive integer $n$, $1+\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{3^2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n^2}<2$.

There are three pegs and $n$ discs of different sizes, initially stacked on the first peg with the largest at the bottom. A move takes the top disc from one peg to another, and a disc may never be placed on a smaller one. Let $M_n$ be the least number of moves needed to transfer the stack to the third peg. (i) Show that $M_n=2M_{n-1}+1$, explaining both why this many moves suffice and why fewer will not do. (ii) Deduce that $M_n=2^n-1$. (iii) Now suppose discs may only move between adjacent pegs (first and second, or second and third). Describe a recursive strategy using $T_n$ moves, where $T_n=3T_{n-1}+2$, and solve this recurrence. (iv) How many legal arrangements of the $n$ discs are there? What does this suggest about the strategy in (iii)?
